lesson.title: Counting Whole Things: Discrete Variables
lesson.summary: This section defines discrete variables as quantitative variables that take only separate, countable values, and works through a worked example using number of siblings recorded for the classroom dataset.
lesson.body:
The previous section established that quantitative variables are numeric measurements that support meaningful arithmetic, and noted that they split into two subtypes. A discrete variable is a quantitative variable whose possible values are separate and countable, typically whole numbers, with clear gaps between one possible value and the next. You cannot land on a value in between two consecutive possibilities. The classic way to recognize a discrete variable is to ask whether the values come from counting. If you are counting something, whether that is people, events, or objects, the result is discrete.

A helpful way to picture this is to imagine every possible value of the variable laid out on a number line. For a discrete variable, those possible values appear as isolated points with real space between them. Number of siblings is a good example: a student can have 0 siblings, 1 sibling, or 2 siblings, but never 1.5 siblings. There is no meaningful value that falls strictly between 1 and 2 in this context. Number of pets, number of cars a family owns, number of correct answers on a multiple choice test, and the quiz score from earlier sections, which can only take whole point values from 0 to 10, are all discrete for the same reason.

It is worth distinguishing a discrete quantitative variable from the numeric codes used for a categorical variable, discussed earlier when a survey coded "yes" as 1 and "no" as 2. Both situations involve whole numbers with gaps between them, but the resemblance stops there. Number of siblings is discrete and quantitative because 0, 1, 2, and 3 represent genuinely different amounts, where 2 siblings really is more siblings than 1, and adding two students' sibling counts together produces a meaningful total number of siblings. The yes and no codes 1 and 2 do not represent amounts of anything at all, and adding them together would be meaningless. The test is not whether the values are whole numbers, but whether those whole numbers measure a real quantity that can sensibly be added, compared, and averaged.

Add a new discrete variable to the running classroom dataset: number of siblings, recorded for each of the 8 students as 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1, 2. Because this variable is discrete and quantitative, computing its average is meaningful even though every individual value is a whole number. Adding the 8 values gives 0 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 10. Dividing by the 8 students gives an average of 10 divided by 8, which equals 1.25 siblings per student. Notice something important here: the average itself, 1.25, is not one of the values any actual student could have. No student has exactly 1.25 siblings, since siblings only come in whole numbers. This is a normal and expected feature of averaging discrete data: the summary statistic can land between the possible individual values, even though no single individual could ever take that in between value.

Because discrete variables take on a limited, countable set of values, they are often displayed using bar graphs or dot plots, where each possible value gets its own clearly separated position, mirroring the real gaps between the possible outcomes. This is different from the graphing approach used for the other subtype of quantitative variable, examined next: continuous variables, whose possible values fill in every point along a range rather than jumping between separated whole numbers.
